title: Wipro Is Buying Back Shares at a 38 Per Cent Premium. Here Is What Every NRI Holder Needs to Know Before June 17.
excerpt: The IT giant's largest-ever buyback opens June 11 at ₹250 per share while the stock trades near ₹180. The math, the deadlines and the catch.
body:
Wipro's ₹15,000 crore share buyback — the largest in the company's history — opens on Wednesday, June 11, and closes on Tuesday, June 17. For NRI shareholders who held the stock on the record date, the window to tender is narrow and the premium is significant.

The buyback price is ₹250 per equity share. As of Tuesday morning, Wipro was trading at approximately ₹180 on the BSE, making the buyback price a 38 per cent premium over market. The company plans to repurchase up to 60 crore fully paid-up equity shares, representing 5.72 per cent of its total paid-up capital.

The board approved the buyback on April 16, shareholders ratified it on May 21, and June 5 was the record date. If your name appeared on Wipro's register as of that date, you are eligible to tender. If you bought shares after June 5, you are not.

## The Entitlement Ratios

Wipro has set two categories. Small shareholders — those holding shares worth up to ₹2 lakh at the buyback price (approximately 800 shares or fewer) — get an entitlement ratio of 11 shares for every 56 held on the record date. That means roughly 19.6 per cent of your holding is eligible for the buyback.

General category shareholders get a less favourable ratio: 10 shares for every 197 held, or about 5.1 per cent. The reserved pool for small shareholders is ₹2,250 crore of the total ₹15,000 crore.

The math matters. If you hold 100 shares in the small shareholder category, your entitlement is approximately 19 shares at ₹250 each, or ₹4,750 — compared to a market value of about ₹3,420 for those same 19 shares. That is roughly ₹1,330 in gross premium per 100 shares held.

## Why This Buyback Exists

The buyback is Wipro's first in nearly three years and arrives at a difficult moment for Indian IT. The company's Q4 FY26 results showed IT services revenue of $2.65 billion, up 2.1 per cent year-on-year, but net profit fell 1.9 per cent to ₹3,522 crore. The Q1 FY27 guidance — flat to negative 2 per cent sequential growth in constant currency — was weaker than analysts expected.

Large deal bookings were a bright spot, surging 65 per cent quarter-on-quarter to $1.44 billion, but the broader picture remains cautious. The US-Iran conflict has dampened enterprise IT spending, AI is reshaping demand patterns, and foreign institutional investors have been selling Indian equities for seven consecutive sessions.

The buyback signals management confidence in the balance sheet, if not in near-term revenue growth. It also functions as a capital return mechanism — reducing the share count, improving earnings per share and return on net worth for continuing shareholders.

## What NRI Shareholders Should Do

**Step one: check eligibility.** If you held Wipro shares on June 5, you are in. American Depositary Share holders needed to have converted their ADSs by June 2 — if you missed that deadline, you cannot participate.

**Step two: decide whether to tender.** At ₹250 against a market price of ₹180, the premium is clear. However, tendering is not all-or-nothing. Your entitlement caps how many shares Wipro will accept from you. You can tender up to your entitlement and keep the rest.

**Step three: submit before June 17.** The tender forms and offer documents are available online and through Wipro's registrar. Physical share certificates, if applicable, must be submitted before the deadline. Verification is expected by June 19, and final acceptance or rejection communicated to stock exchanges by June 23.

## Tax Implications for NRIs

Buyback proceeds are subject to a 20 per cent tax on the distributed income under Section 115QA of the Income Tax Act, payable by the company. For NRIs, there is no additional tax liability on the buyback amount received — it is effectively tax-free in the shareholder's hands.

However, capital gains implications depend on when you acquired the shares. If you bought at a price higher than ₹250, the buyback represents a crystallised loss. If you bought below ₹250, the entire spread is profit, and the company's tax payment covers it. Consult your CA or tax adviser for your specific holding.

## The Bigger Picture

Wipro's buyback is not happening in isolation. Indian IT is navigating a structural transition from labour-arbitrage services to AI-augmented delivery, and the stock prices of Wipro, TCS and Infosys have all come under pressure. Wipro shares are trading near three-year lows.

For NRI investors, this is a moment of decision. The buyback offers a guaranteed premium on a limited number of shares. Whether you participate depends on your cost basis, your tax situation and your view on Wipro's medium-term trajectory. The numbers, at least, are clear. The window closes June 17.
